analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income taxes with a 17% flat tax and repeals the estate tax.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill, introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would throw out the current income tax and replace it with one 17% rate on a narrow base of income: wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits. Investment income like capital gains, dividends, and interest would no longer be taxed at all. It would repeal the estate and gift taxes, every income tax credit including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, and the alternative minimum tax, and it would require a 60% vote of Congress to ever change the new tax system.
analysis.who_benefits: Households whose income comes from investments (capital gains, dividends, interest) would pay no tax on that income at all, since the bill defines taxable income to include only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation. The largest estates would pay nothing under the repealed estate and gift tax. Businesses would pay 17% on a value-added-style base with deductions for business inputs, replacing the current corporate tax. Higher-paid employees would also benefit from the repeal of pension nondiscrimination rules and the tax on employers reclaiming pension surpluses.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a single 17% rate on individual taxable income, defined only as wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction, so income from capital gains, dividends, and interest would not be taxed.
Repeals the estate, gift, and generation-skipping transfer taxes, applying retroactively to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2017.

Repeals all income tax credits, the alternative minimum tax, and most income tax provisions, and replaces the corporate income tax with a 17% tax on business activity with deductions for business inputs.
Repeals pension nondiscrimination rules, contribution limits, and distribution restrictions, and allows employers to transfer excess pension assets to themselves with only ordinary income inclusion.

Locks in the new system by making it out of order for Congress to consider any tax change that raises a rate, adds a rate, cuts the standard deduction, or reduces revenue, unless three-fifths of each chamber vote to allow it.

analysis.who_pays: Working households would carry the tax load: wages are the core of the new tax base, and every income tax credit would disappear, including the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit that offset taxes for low- and moderate-income families. The loss of estate, investment-income, and business taxes would substantially cut federal revenue, meaning either larger deficits or cuts to government services. Current rules that stop company retirement plans from favoring highly paid employees would be gone.

drawbacks.text: Repealing every income tax credit would eliminate the Earned Income Tax Credit and Child Tax Credit, which offset or erase federal tax liability for millions of low- and moderate-income working families.

Because taxable income would exclude capital gains, dividends, and interest, a household living entirely off investments would owe no federal income tax, while the tax base rests almost entirely on wages.
The estate, gift, and generation-skipping tax repeal would apply retroactively to deaths and gifts after December 31, 2017, benefiting the heirs of people who already died under the old law.

The bill would repeal the rules that keep company retirement plans from discriminating in favor of highly compensated employees and let employers reclaim excess pension plan assets, reducing protections for rank-and-file workers' retirement benefits.
The supermajority lock-in would make nearly any future tax change, including closing loopholes, require a 60% vote in each chamber rather than a simple majority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers large, permanent gains concentrated at the top — untaxed investment income, no estate tax, a lower and broader-deducted business tax — while shifting the federal tax base almost entirely onto wages and stripping out the credits that working families rely on. Its simplification appeal is real, but the redistribution runs uphill, and the supermajority rule would make the system nearly impossible to revise.

outcome.mechanism: Sen. Shelby introduced the bill in April 2019 and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it before the two-year Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Shelby introduced the SMART Act on April 11, 2019, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee took no further action, and the bill received no vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Everyday taxpayers kept the existing progressive tax code, its credits, and the estate tax; wealthy households and large estates simply lost the opportunity this bill would have created, and it cost them nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Everyday taxpayers; the bill never advanced

for.name: Sen. Richard Shelby
for.role: U.S. Senator from Alabama; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the flat tax bill and submitted it to the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to itself and never scheduled a markup or vote during the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party.

industries.note: Investment income would go untaxed, the estate and gift tax would disappear retroactively, and the remaining tax base would fall on wages. Ordinary wage earners would bear a larger share of federal taxation.

industries.industry: Large employers with defined-benefit pension plans
industries.note: Employers could move excess pension assets back to themselves with minimal tax, and pension rules against favoring executives would be repealed. The savings would come at the expense of plan participants' protections.

The corporate tax would be replaced with a 17% tax on business activity with deductions for inputs, a broad simplification. Businesses would also pay a 17% tax on noncash fringe benefits provided to employees, a new cost.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Replacing a large share of the tax code with a single flat rate and standard deduction would dramatically shrink the market for filing help and compliance software, a cost to the industry that mirrors a gain for ordinary filers.
